source.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
source.authors: David Bau; Bo-Lei Zhou; A. Khosla; A. Oliva; A. Torralba

page_placements.theme: Architecture, width, sparsity and training change counts of concept-aligned units or superposition proxies
Neuron basis is privileged by the activation function and training; rotation removes unit-level interpretability

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how many visual concepts align with individual CNN units and tests how this measure changes across architectures and training conditions. This is a different operational measure from directly counting neurons with unrelated responses.
record.gate_note: The study does not directly measure the prevalence of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. It scores unit–concept alignment using Broden and reports unique-detector counts; those counts are an interpretability proxy, not a polysemantic-neuron rate. The text reports an 80% reduction after rotation, but rotation results are not linked to a listed version because they do not measure unrelated inputs or their shared features.
record.test_reason: The study counts unique Broden concepts matched to units, taking only each unit's top-ranked label. It never measures whether units respond to several unrelated inputs, so it reports no polysemantic-neuron rate. Its architecture, training and width effects concern a related construct, single-unit concept alignment, and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that interpretability is axis-aligned, not an inevitable result of discriminative power, consistent with a partially disentangled representation. They also conclude that layers disentangle different concept categories and that training techniques significantly affect unit interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: Uses dense concept annotations and unit-to-concept IoU segmentation scores, rather than the original source’s neuron visualization approach. It counts unique concept detectors as its layer-level measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The detector counts vary with architecture, training dataset, dropout, batch normalization and layer width. The method uses a fixed top-activation quantile and an IoU cutoff; the authors say qualitative results are insensitive to IoU threshold, while different thresholds produce different detector counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Random orthogonal rotation of AlexNet conv5 cuts unique detectors by 80% while discriminative power is unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-unit interpretability is basis-aligned and not implied by discriminative power.

fits_no_version.finding: Unique-detector counts rank ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet and Places > ImageNet. Batch norm lowers them, removing dropout shifts them from objects to textures, and random initializations give similar counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The number of units aligned with human concepts depends on architecture, training data and training technique.

fits_no_version.finding: Widening conv5 from 256 to 768 units increases detectors at about 0.5% lower top-1 accuracy. Going to 1024 or 2048 units gives no further significant gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer width increases concept-aligned units, up to a plateau.

record.problems: Unique-detector counts are a proxy for interpretability, not a direct measurement of polysemantic neurons or unrelated input responses. Many plotted values are only in figures; numerical values and uncertainty estimates are not stated. The Broden-based measure is limited to concepts represented in that dataset.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows retained. Figure 10 reports detector evolution over training iterations, but the study does not give exact plotted values in text and this result does not directly measure any listed version's polysemantic-neuron claim.

untested.parts: No measurement of units responding to multiple unrelated inputs. The Fig. 6 caption gives only an anecdote (horses and dogs; white ellipsoids and jets).
No test of superposition or of features outnumbering neurons.
No share of polysemantic neurons reported under any architecture or training change.
Not tested. Authors call the Fig. 6 mixed units 'concept generalizations' without analysis.
Threshold sensitivity is mentioned only for detector counts, not for polysemanticity.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V5 supports label is not justified. The method assigns one top label per unit and never counts units with unrelated responses, so the record's own gate_note contradicts its labels. The Fig. 6 caption anecdote is qualitative only: GoogLeNet 4e unit 225 fires on horses and dogs, and unit 759 on white ellipsoids and jets.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated kinds of input.
No language models or token/context responses are studied.
Layer width is varied, but the study does not test whether features outnumber neurons or whether superposition causes polysemanticity.
Does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Measures unique concept detectors rather than the share of polysemantic neurons. Does not test SoLU or whether polysemanticity itself can be lowered without a large performance loss.
Does not investigate whether canonical polysemantic neurons actually detect one shared feature or related offshoots.
Uses a fixed activation quantile and IoU criterion; it does not report a systematic comparison of results across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It measures a related construct, interpretability as axis alignment. It notes in passing that a unit may detect multiple concepts, but it does not measure polysemantic neurons.

tranche.reason: The study measures axis-aligned single-unit concept alignment (unique detectors). It keeps only each unit's top-ranked label even though a unit may detect several concepts, and reports no rate of units responding to several unrelated inputs. So it does not test the polysemanticity claim.

source_check.notes: Both rows and both statements match the text. The rotation result (80% fewer unique detectors) and the width result concern axis-aligned interpretability and detector counts, not polysemanticity. Network Dissection keeps only each unit's top label (Sec. 2.2), so it cannot give a polysemantic-unit share. No verdicts are listed.

statements.correction: AlexNet-GAP-Wide (conv5 256 to 768, FC removed, GAP, Places365): top-1 0.5% lower than standard AlexNet, many more unique detectors and detector units. 1024 and 2048 units: unique concepts do not significantly increase further.
statements.problem: Minor: the wide model is AlexNet with FC layers removed plus a GAP layer, trained on Places365, so the change is more than widening alone. The 0.5% figure is top-1 accuracy relative to standard AlexNet. The no-further-gain result for 1024 and 2048 refers to unique concepts.

statements.correction: AlexNet conv5 on Places205: a random orthogonal rotation gives 80% fewer unique detectors. Discriminative power is exactly the same.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Unique-detector counts differ by architecture, and the text reports more detectors for Places than ImageNet training; these are interpretability-proxy results, not direct polysemantic-neuron rates (r1–r8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Dropout, batch normalization, width and random initialization comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Training-condition effects vary: removing dropout shifts detector categories in opposite directions, batch normalization reduces interpretability, widening increases detector counts with similar accuracy, and random initializations converge to similar levels (r9–r15). These findings do not establish changes in the share of polysemantic neurons.
